nameStory: This plant earned its name "miner's lettuce" during the California Gold Rush of the 1840s, when miners discovered they could eat its tender, succulent leaves to prevent scurvy. The miners valued this vitamin C-rich green so highly that it became their go-to salad crop, leading to its enduring common name.
description: Miner's lettuce is a small, fleshy annual herb that looks quite different from typical New England wildflowers. The plant grows low to the ground in a rosette pattern, rarely exceeding 6 inches tall. Its most distinctive feature is the way its round, disk-like upper leaves appear to be pierced by the stem, creating a unique "perforated" look. The succulent leaves feel thick and slightly rubbery to the touch, similar to jade plant leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Upper leaves are perfectly round and appear to be pierced through the center by the stem, creating a distinctive disk effect. The leaves feel thick, fleshy, and slightly cool to the touch, like small green coins made of soft rubber.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or pale pink flowers emerge from above the disk-like leaves in small clusters. Each flower has 5 delicate petals and is only about 1/8 inch across, requiring close examination to see clearly.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low rosettes or spreads as a mat close to the ground. The entire plant rarely grows taller than your hand, giving it a prostrate, carpet-like appearance.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Stems are smooth, somewhat translucent, and appear to pierce directly through the center of the upper round leaves. The stems feel slightly sticky when broken and may have a faint cucumber-like scent.

habitat: In New England, miner's lettuce is quite rare and typically found in disturbed soils, gardens, and occasionally along paths or roadsides where it may have escaped cultivation. It prefers moist, rich soil and partial shade, often appearing in areas where the ground has been recently disturbed or in compost-enriched garden beds.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic disk leaves. This is the best time to spot the distinctive perforated leaf structure as plants begin flowering.
seasonality.summer: Plants may continue growing in cool, moist locations but often die back during hot, dry periods. Look for the tiny white flowers during early summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and plants typically complete their life cycle. In mild areas, new seedlings may germinate and establish small rosettes.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants have died, but in protected locations with mild microclimates, some plants may persist as small rosettes under snow cover.

funFact: Despite being native to the western United States, miner's lettuce is completely edible and tastes like a cross between spinach and cucumber - you can eat it right in the field as a trail snack, and it's actually more nutritious than regular lettuce!
confusionNotes: The perforated disk leaves make this plant virtually impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. No other plant in our region has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem in this distinctive way.
contextualKnowledge: Though called "winter purslane" in some regions, this plant is unrelated to true purslane (Portulaca oleracea). The name simply refers to both plants being edible, succulent greens that can grow in cool weather.
compareHints: Unlike its spring beauty relatives (Carolina and Virginia springbeauty), miner's lettuce has the unique disk-shaped upper leaves that appear pierced by the stem, while the other Claytonia species have narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in pairs. The spring beauties also have much showier pink-striped flowers compared to miner's lettuce's tiny white blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Carolina Springbeauty differs from Virginia Springbeauty mainly in its leaf shape - Carolina has broad, oval leaves while Virginia has narrow, linear leaves that look almost grass-like.
Virginia Springbeauty differs from its cousin Carolina Springbeauty mainly in leaf shape - Virginia has very narrow, grasslike leaves while Carolina has broader oval leaves.
